concept.name: Last point of supply
concept.definition: The Wyckoff event (LPSY) in which a feeble rally on narrow spread follows a sign of weakness, showing the market's inability to advance because of weak demand, substantial supply, or both. LPSYs represent the final waves of large operators' distribution and preferred areas for short entries before markdown.
concept.intuition: After support breaks, the market stages one last tired bounce — the final chance to get out or get short before the drop.
concept.mechanics: Following a SOW, rallies are monitored for narrow spread and low volume, indicating exhausted demand; such rallies that fail at or below the broken support (ice) are labeled LPSYs. Despite the singular name, multiple LPSYs can occur during Phase D of distribution.
concept.failure_modes: A rally labeled LPSY can regain strength and climb back into or above the range, invalidating the markdown scenario; the label is confirmed only by subsequent weakness.
concept.misconceptions: The LPSY is not necessarily the last rally ever, nor a precise price; it is a zone identified by narrow spread and poor volume on the rally, not by an exact level.
concept.example: After breaking support at 136, a stock bounces to 138 over four days on shrinking volume and small ranges; the trader shorts there with a stop above the ice, treating the bounce as an LPSY.

citations.source: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett)
